errors: In the momentum line the transcription has rho instead of rho1 (or rho2) in front of (x'1 - dx/dt); this is probably the manuscript's own abbreviation. It is harmless, since rho1(u1-U) = rho2(u2-U).
The ± in U = u1 ± a sqrt(rho2/rho1) = u2 ± a sqrt(rho1/rho2) must be taken with the same sign in both expressions. This is implicit but correct.

The 'loss of vis viva' a^2(rho1+rho2)(u1-u2)/2 balances only kinetic energy against pressure work. It omits the change in the isothermal gas's compressional (free) energy, so it is not the full dissipation. Its sign criterion (positive iff u1 > u2) is nevertheless right.

The expressions (-s-1+4p)a and (s+1+4q)a for u ∓ a cannot be checked from this page. Taken at face value, their difference would force q - p = -(s)/2 + const, so they presumably refer to a specific example or parametrisation.
The dw'/dq' computation in Part A has cramped limits and boundary terms; individual signs cannot be confirmed. The overall structure (integral over the data curve plus boundary terms) is correct.

results.what: Adjoint equation with characteristic boundary conditions v_p+v=0 on q=q', v_q-v=0 on p=p', v(p',q')=1, and the resulting integral representation of the solution of w_pq - w_q + w_p = 0
results.modern_name: Riemann's method / Riemann(-Green) function for linear hyperbolic equations

results.what: Jump conditions rho1(u1-U)=rho2(u2-U), a^2(rho1-rho2)=m(u2-u1), giving m^2=a^2 rho1 rho2 and U = u1 ± a sqrt(rho2/rho1)
A discontinuity persists only if compressive (u1>u2); compressions steepen into shocks in finite time, rarefactions spread
results.modern_name: Admissibility / Lax entropy condition; gradient catastrophe

results.what: Energy dissipated at the shock equals a^2(rho1+rho2)(u1-u2)/2, positive exactly for admissible shocks
results.modern_name: Energy dissipation at shocks as admissibility criterion

results.what: Classification of the decay of an initial jump into two shocks, two rarefactions, or shock+rarefaction, with explicit isothermal thresholds
results.modern_name: Riemann problem for isothermal gas dynamics

deep.surprise_reason: The contents (Riemann function, shock conditions, compressive admissibility, solution of the Riemann problem) are known from Riemann's 1860 paper. What is mildly notable is the dating: the Riemann-function method in June 1856 and the shock analysis in October 1857. Also notable is the explicit kinetic-energy-loss computation as a sign criterion for admissible shocks, which, as far as I know, is not in the published paper.

checkable.asserts: My closed-form Riemann function satisfies the adjoint equation v_pq + v_q - v_p = 0 (should be 0).
The characteristic condition v_p + v = 0 holds on q = q'.

checkable.sympy: r1,r2,a,u1,u2,U=symbols('r1 r2 a u1 u2 U',positive=True); m=a*sqrt(r1*r2); solve([r1*(u1-U)-m, r2*(u2-U)-m],[u1,u2])
checkable.asserts: u1-U = a*sqrt(r2/r1) and u2-U = a*sqrt(r1/r2) when m = a*sqrt(r1 r2).
Momentum balance a^2(rho1-rho2) = m(u2-u1) is satisfied for m^2 = a^2 rho1 rho2 (should be 0).
Pressure work minus vis-viva gain equals a^2(rho1+rho2)(u1-u2)/2 (should be 0).
The two-shock threshold at rho* = rho2 gives u1-u2 = a(rho2-rho1)/sqrt(rho1 rho2), matching (u1-u2)^2 > a^2(rho1-rho2)^2/(rho1 rho2) (should be 0).
The two-rarefaction threshold is u2-u1 = a|log(rho1/rho2)| (should be 0).

transcription_corrections: In the momentum line the transcription's 'rho' is presumably rho1 (or rho2), since the factor is the mass flux rho1(x'1 - dx/dt); confirm against the image.

The first energy line ('Verlust [?] an lebendiger Kraft ... (x'2^2 - x'1^2)/2') is probably 'Zuwachs' (gain), not 'Verlust'. The separate later line gives the loss as the difference with the work done ('geleistete Arbeit').
In the next-to-last paragraph, 'die Richtungen umgekehrt' is plausibly 'Richtungen vertauscht'; either way the meaning is reversed directions for rho1 < rho2.

The integral limits in Part A, written 's,p'' and 's,q'', denote points (s,p') and (s,q') on the data line. The transcription's '∫_{q,s}' should likely read '∫_{p,s}' / '∫_{s,q}'; the limits are hard to read.
